questions.stem: In persuasion, an appeal to ethos works by:
options: using facts, evidence and logical reasoning to convince
repeating the same phrase at the start of each sentence
building the speaker's credibility and trustworthiness
stirring the audience's emotions, such as fear or pity
questions.explanation: Ethos is about character: the audience is persuaded because they trust the speaker, for example a doctor speaking about health. Stirring emotions is pathos, and using evidence and reasoning is logos. Writers often combine all three in a single speech.

questions.stem: A speaker says: 'Our survey of 400 students found that seven in ten skip breakfast, and those students scored lower in morning tests.' This mainly appeals to:
options: logos, through evidence and reasoning
pathos, through emotional language
ethos, through the speaker's reputation
tradition, through how things used to be
questions.explanation: Logos persuades with facts, figures and logical links, here survey data connected to test results. The sentence uses no emotionally loaded words, so it is not mainly pathos. A careful reader would still ask how the survey was done before accepting the conclusion.

questions.stem: Which sentence relies most on pathos?
options: Picture a tiny, shivering puppy, left in the rain, waiting for someone to care.
Adopting from a shelter costs less than buying from a breeder, council figures show.
As a vet with twenty years of experience, I have seen the benefits of adoption.
Adoption reduces the number of animals kept in overcrowded shelters each year.
questions.explanation: Pathos appeals to the audience's feelings, and words like 'tiny', 'shivering' and 'waiting for someone to care' are chosen to stir pity. Council figures appeal to logos and the vet's experience appeals to ethos. Pathos is powerful because readers often feel before they think.

questions.stem: 'Install solar panels now and watch your power bills shrink year after year.' Which appeal is this?
options: An appeal to patriotism
An appeal to tradition
An appeal to fairness and justice
An appeal to self-interest
questions.explanation: An appeal to self-interest, sometimes called a hip-pocket appeal, persuades by showing the audience what they personally gain, here money saved. Patriotism would appeal to love of country. Self-interest appeals are common in advertising because 'what's in it for me?' is a strong motivator.

questions.stem: 'If we do nothing, the next fire season could take your home, your town, everything.' Which appeal is this?
options: An appeal to fear
An appeal to tradition
An appeal to patriotism
An appeal to authority
questions.explanation: An appeal to fear warns the audience of a frightening outcome if they do not act. The threat of losing a home and a whole town is designed to create urgency. Fear can be effective, but readers should check whether the danger described is realistic.

questions.stem: 'For over a hundred years, this town has held its show in the same paddock, and we should not change that now.' Which appeal is this?
options: An appeal to expert authority
An appeal to tradition
An appeal to fairness
An appeal to self-interest
questions.explanation: An appeal to tradition argues that something should continue because it has always been done that way. Here the hundred-year history is the whole argument. A critical reader might point out that 'we have always done it' is not, by itself, a reason that it is best.

questions.stem: 'We will build it, we will fund it, and we will finish it.' What is this three-part structure called?
options: Understatement, a deliberate downplaying
A tricolon, or the rule of three
Antithesis, a balance of opposites
Euphemism, a softened expression
questions.explanation: A tricolon groups ideas in threes, which sounds complete, rhythmic and memorable. This example also repeats 'we will' at the start of each part, which is anaphora. Antithesis would set two opposite ideas against each other instead.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses anaphora?
options: Without cleaner air, our streets will never feel truly safe again.
Action is needed now, before the air grows any dirtier than this.
We need cleaner air. We need safer streets. We need action now.
Clean air, safe streets and fast action are exactly what we need.
questions.explanation: Anaphora repeats the same word or phrase at the start of successive sentences or clauses, here 'We need'. The list of clean air, safe streets and fast action is a group of three, but it does not repeat an opening phrase. Anaphora builds rhythm and drives the main idea home.

questions.stem: Which sentence is an example of antithesis?
options: Making a promise is something we all do every day.
Promises, promises: they are made all the time.
It is easy to make promises, but hard to keep them.
It is easy, simple and quick to make a promise today.
questions.explanation: Antithesis places opposite ideas in balanced, parallel phrases, here 'easy to make' against 'hard to keep'. The sentence listing 'easy, simple and quick' is a group of three similar words, not opposites. Antithesis makes a contrast sharp and quotable.

questions.stem: 'Teenagers today never read books.' Why is this a weak argument?
options: It quotes an expert who is not qualified to comment on reading
It is a sweeping generalisation that ignores teenagers who do
It uses statistics that are far too precise for readers to believe
It attacks the character of a person who disagrees with the claim
questions.explanation: A generalisation makes a claim about a whole group based on some members, and words like 'never', 'always' and 'all' are warning signs. The sentence contains no statistics or experts at all. One reader who loves books is enough to disprove 'never'.

questions.stem: In a debate about a new skate park, a speaker says: 'My opponent is always late to class, so his ideas about the park can't be trusted.' This is:
options: an anecdote drawn from the speaker's own experience
a rebuttal of the opponent's actual evidence and claims
an ad hominem attack on the person, not the argument
an appeal to logos that uses clear and careful reasoning
questions.explanation: Ad hominem is Latin for 'to the person': it attacks the opponent's character instead of answering their argument. Being late to class has nothing to do with whether the skate park idea is good. A genuine rebuttal would deal with the evidence the opponent actually gave.

questions.stem: A critic calls a new apartment block 'a concrete shoebox for battery hens'. Using harsh words to make something sound worse than it is, is called:
options: understatement
antithesis
dysphemism
euphemism
questions.explanation: Dysphemism is the opposite of euphemism: it swaps a neutral term for an insulting one. A euphemism would soften the description, such as calling small flats 'cosy, compact living'. Both techniques reveal the writer's attitude through word choice.

questions.stem: 'This decision will destroy every small business in the state overnight.' Which technique is this?
options: Antithesis
Hyperbole
Understatement
Euphemism
questions.explanation: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect, and 'every' business 'overnight' is far beyond what could literally happen. Understatement does the opposite, making something sound smaller than it is. Hyperbole can grab attention, but too much of it can make a writer seem unreliable.

questions.stem: Which sentence is objective rather than subjective?
options: The new library opened on 3 March and holds 40 000 books.
The new library is a stunning gift to our lucky community.
Sadly, the new library is far too small for our needs.
Everyone will surely love the bright new library.
questions.explanation: Objective language states facts that can be checked, without the writer's feelings. Words like 'stunning', 'lucky', 'sadly' and 'surely' reveal opinions, which makes the other sentences subjective. Persuasive writers often mix both, using facts to make their opinions seem stronger.

questions.stem: A speech ends: 'Sign the petition today. Tell your friends. Make your voice heard.' What do these sentences use?
options: Statistics providing objective evidence
Imperatives that make a call to action
Rhetorical questions inviting reflection
Euphemisms softening a harsh truth
questions.explanation: Each sentence begins with a command verb, sign, tell, make, so the audience is told exactly what to do. A call to action at the end of a persuasive text turns agreement into action. Rhetorical questions would end with question marks and ask rather than instruct.

questions.stem: 'You know what it's like to wait for a bus that never comes.' Which technique is this?
options: Antithesis, balancing opposite ideas
Direct address, speaking to the audience as 'you'
Inclusive language, using 'we' and 'us' to unite people
An appeal to tradition and the past
questions.explanation: Direct address speaks straight to the audience with 'you', which makes the argument feel personal and draws on their own experience. Inclusive language uses 'we' and 'us' to place the writer and audience on the same side. Both create a sense of connection, but through different pronouns.

questions.stem: Which sentence acknowledges a counterargument and then refutes it?
options: Uniforms are the best choice for every school because they look smart and save time in the morning.
Some say uniforms limit self-expression, and I think they make a very good point about it.
Uniforms limit self-expression and creativity, so they should be removed from every single school.
Some say uniforms limit self-expression; however, students still express it through their ideas.
questions.explanation: Refutation means raising the opposing view and then answering it, signalled here by 'however'. The sentence that agrees the critics 'make a very good point' acknowledges the other side but concedes rather than refuting. Dealing with counterarguments makes a writer seem fair and confident.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an exposition and a discussion?
options: An exposition is always spoken aloud; a discussion is always written down on paper
An exposition uses no evidence at all; a discussion uses only statistics as evidence
An exposition argues one side; a discussion weighs several sides before concluding
An exposition tells a story in time order; a discussion explains how something works
questions.explanation: Both are argument text types, but an exposition takes one position and argues for it, while a discussion weighs up different viewpoints before reaching a conclusion or recommendation. Telling a story in time order describes a narrative or recount. Either type can be spoken or written.

questions.stem: Which essay task asks for a discursive response?
options: Explore different views on social media's effect on friendship.
Argue that social media should be banned for anyone under sixteen.
Explain the steps for setting up a new social media account.
Retell a time social media helped you make a new friend.
questions.explanation: A discursive text explores a topic from several angles, often in a reflective tone, without having to argue firmly for one side. 'Argue that' asks for an exposition with a single position. The explaining and retelling tasks ask for procedural and recount writing.

questions.stem: 'Top surgeon Dr Lin says this sports drink boosts brain power.' Why might a careful reader be sceptical?
options: The claim relies on a rhetorical question rather than on evidence
The sentence is objective, so it cannot possibly be trying to persuade anyone
A surgeon's expertise may not cover nutrition, so the authority is misused
Experts should never be quoted in persuasive writing of any kind at all
questions.explanation: An appeal to authority is only as strong as the expert's knowledge of the topic, and surgery is not nutrition or brain science. Quoting experts is a legitimate technique when the expert actually knows the field. Always ask whether the authority is relevant, not just impressive.
